resources.string: Practice mode: type in the language you\'re learning and it goes out in your language, while the bar above the keys shows what you typed. Direct mode: type in your own language as usual, and the bar shows it live in the language you\'re learning. The ES | EN switch above the keys shows which language you\'re typing in; tap the other one to change.
Language for these settings and the keyboard\'s messages
Language I\'m learning (what I type in practice mode)
My language (what gets sent, and what I type in direct mode)
There\'s no %1$s keyboard layout yet, so you\'ll get QWERTY.
In direct mode you type in %1$s, so the keys switch to its layout.
Language packs ready ✓ — translation works offline.
Language packs need downloading (about 30 MB each).
Slide across the letters to type a word, without lifting your finger.
Word suggestions above the keys. Ignores accents, so typing \"cancion\" offers \"canción\".
Fixes typos and missing accents when you press space. Backspace straight after undoes it.
Word lists: FrequencyWords by Hermit Dave, from OpenSubtitles, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Puts a red squiggly line under misspelt words and missing accents in the practice bar. Tap the word to see the fix. Also catches some gender mistakes like “la problema” or “este es una” in Spanish, Portuguese and Italian (blue line). Works offline.

Also checks grammar, like gender agreement and verb forms (blue squiggly line), and explains each mistake. Sends the text in the practice bar to LanguageTool (languagetool.org) when you pause typing. Free, no account. Only your practice text is sent, not the translation.
Tap here and type with Language Keyboard

Tips: the ✓ key (where Enter usually is) locks in the current translation. Tap EN on the ES | EN switch for direct mode: type straight in your own language and see it in the language you\'re learning above the keys. Tap ES to go back. Tap a suggestion to use it; tap your own word (in quotes) to keep it and teach it to the keyboard. Hold and slide along the space bar to move the cursor. Long-press a letter for accents. Use the 🌐 button under the keyboard to switch keyboards.

“%1$s” is %2$s, even though it ends in -%3$s (one to remember)
“%1$s” is %2$s (one to learn with its article: “%3$s”)
“%1$s” is feminine, but because it starts with a stressed “a” it takes “el” or “un” in the singular (“el agua”, but “las aguas”)
Use “%1$s”, not “%2$s”: %3$s, and %4$s has to match the noun it’s about.
“%1$s” is a real word, but not a noun. After “%3$s” you probably mean “%2$s”.
